title: Vuelta a España 2026 podium watch: Who’s still in the race for the top three?
content:

Vuelta a España 2026 podium watch: Who’s still in the race for the top three?

We’re just over the halfway mark at this year’s Vuelta a España, and everything is up in the air when it comes to the top five in the general classification. Who’d have thought?

After Tadej Pogačar abandoned the Spanish race last weekend, Enric Mas has taken over the red jersey after eleven stages. The Spaniard, a four-time podium finisher at the Vuelta, now sits 1min 16sec ahead of four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič and 1min 39sec ahead of Felix Gall. Beyond those three, the top eight in GC right now all have a chance of making the final podium.

Let’s get to know the band of eight podium challengers and weigh up their strengths and weaknesses coming into the next wave of GC stages.

Enric Mas

After years of being on the podium, Mas is in a realistic position to win this race overall. The Movistar leader assumed the race lead after Pogačar crashed out, and he’s seemed the strongest ever since.

This has been most evident on the climbs. Not only did he manage to get the win on Stage 9, but Mas was bold enough to follow Pogačar’s move on Stage 6, stealing a valuable minute on most of his rivals.

Mas should continue to extend his lead in the high mountain stages to come, but there are some worries about his time-trialling potential. His team strength has also been weak when the race enters key points, but Mas’s metronomic style makes it hard to imagine any big meltdowns during the final week of racing.

Enric Mas overview

  • Current position overall: 1st
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 2nd (Vuelta a España 2018, 2021, 2022)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 1st (2022, 2023)

Enric Mas’ key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 50th
  • Stage 4: 6th
  • Stage 6: 2nd
  • Stage 7: 21st
  • Stage 9: 1st

Primož Roglič

Roglič is considered by some to be the closest rival to Mas’s lead right now. Before Stage 12, he was positioned just over a minute behind the Spaniard.

The Slovenian has won four Vueltas, and he knows his way around this race. He’s often kept his powder dry, but this year he seems to be slowly growing into the race. His form might have been poor on the run-up, but he’s looking stronger than many expected in the mountains. If he’s got his sprinting legs back, he’s also likely to pick up some bonus seconds at stage finishes.

Roglič has weak team support, but he’s managed to roll with the punches so far. Unlike many of the frontrunners, Roglič will relish the prospect of a time-trial. As a previous Olympic champion, he’s a dab hand against the clock. However, he only managed to gain eight seconds on Mas in a time-trial a third of the length of the one that could end up deciding this Vuelta a España.

Primož Roglič overview

  • Current position overall: 2nd (1min 18sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 1st (Vuelta a España 2019, 2020, 2021, 2024, Giro d’Italia 2023)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 1st (2019, 2020, 2021, 2024)

Primož Roglič’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 24th (8s ahead of Mas)
  • Stage 4: 7th (0s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 7th (46s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 23rd (13s behind Mas)
  • Stage 9: 3rd (12s behind Mas)

Felix Gall

On the back of his first Grand Tour podium at the Giro back in the spring, Gall looks set to be in the fight for another podium here at the Vuelta.

Despite a poor opening time-trial, Gall has been the closest rival to Mas in the mountains. Besides Mas’s big runaway move on Stage 6, Gall has lost just 21 seconds in the mountains so far. If he manages to cling on and limit his losses against the clock, Gall should be in with a shout of adding a Vuelta podium to his big Giro splash earlier this year.

Gall looks to have the strongest team at the moment. Gregor Muhlberger in particular has been a key element on mountain stages. However, some have lumped criticism that Decathlon CMA CGM have launched Gall too early.

Felix Gall overview

  • Current position overall: 3rd (1min 39sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 2nd (Giro d’Italia 2026)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 8th (2025)

Felix Gall’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 91st (13s behind Mas)
  • Stage 4: 3rd (0s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 6th (46s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 20th (3s ahead of Mas)
  • Stage 9: 4th (18s behind Mas)

Oscar Onley

British hopes are pinned on Oscar Onley, who looks on track to replicate the top five finish he pulled off at the Tour de France in 2025.

So far, Onley has been a mixed bag, with more highs than lows, in fairness. Onley lost a huge chunk of time on Stage 6, having experienced some digestive problems during the race. However, he quickly bounced back and looked particularly promising on Stage 9, when he stuck to Mas’s wheel to the finish.

Onley will struggle in the race’s long 30km time-trial in the final week. Plus, his team support seems to be minimal, with the likes of Carlos Rodríguez underperforming. Having been on Picnic PostNL for a long while, Onley’s used to fending for himself in the mountains. Come the final week, when the leading group will be ripped apart by attrition, Onley could thrive.

Oscar Onley overview

  • Current position overall: 4th (2min 20sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 4th (Tour de France 2025)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: DNF

Oscar Onley’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 106th (17s behind Mas)
  • Stage 4: 4th (0s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 12th (1min 38s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 24th (13s behind Mas)
  • Stage 9: 2nd (0s behind Mas)

Richard Carapaz

Richard Carapaz has been a bit of a yo-yo at this Vuelta. Sometimes he’s been up for the fight, sometimes he’s been swallowed up. That means he finds himself in fifth, over three minutes behind Enric Mas.

The Ecuadorian can sometimes come alive in the final week of racing, just as we saw in this year’s Tour de France. He’s also searching for a new contract, so the pressure is on for Carapaz to perform.

Like many of the other big players, Carapaz isn’t a natural against the clock. However, his rugged climbing style could see him launch some bold moves during the Vuelta’s tougher mountain stages.

Richard Carapaz overview

  • Current position overall: 5th (3min 26sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 1st (Giro d’Italia 2019)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 2nd (2020)

Richard Carapaz’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 52nd (0s behind Mas)
  • Stage 4: 8th (0s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 4th (46s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 30th (1min 6s behind Mas)
  • Stage 9: 9th (54s behind Mas)

Mattias Skjelmose

You’re forgiven for not realising Mattias Skjelmose was here. His presence has been rather unremarkable so far, but he’s still in the mix, sitting in sixth at almost four minutes behind the race leader.

The Dane hasn’t been as sprightly here as he was at the Tour de France. In the mountains, he’s been trailing behind Mas and most favourites. He lost over a minute on both Stage 6 and 7. However, his performance on Stage 9 showed more promise. Skjelmose is well-tested, on the other hand, and could find himself clawing back time in the final week. He’s not averse to an all-or-nothing attack, after all.

While the Vuelta unravels, Skjelmose might be subject to another transfer battle, as rumours suggest he could be looking for the exit door from Lidl-Trek, who have too many cooks in the kitchen for Skjelmose to feel satisfied.

Mattias Skjelmose overview

  • Current position overall: 6th (3min 55sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 5th (Vuelta a España 2024)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 5th (2024)

Mattias Skjelmose’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 40th (4s ahead of Mas)
  • Stage 4: 9th (38s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 10th (1min 38s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 28th (1min 6s behind Mas)
  • Stage 9: 6th (20s behind Mas)

Sepp Kuss

Besides Roglič, Sepp Kuss is another Vuelta champion looking for something to write home about at this year’s edition.

For a while, Kuss was in fourth place overall. Perhaps this was down to the home advantage provided by passing his home in Andorra, but the American would soon lose a lot of time on the following GC stages. That was until he started to lose time during the second half of week one.

He doesn’t have the same kick as some of the other contenders on this list. Neither does he have the pedigree against the clock to feel confident ahead of the big time-trial during the final week. Where Kuss could thrive however is through his experience and consistency in big three-week races. That said, he’s never been the out-and-out leader in a situation like this before. Not even in 2023, when he won the whole thing.

Sepp Kuss overview

  • Current position overall: 7th (4min 09sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 1st (Vuelta a España 2023)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 1st (2023)

Sepp Kuss’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 89th (12s behind Mas)
  • Stage 4: 5th (0s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 11th (1min 38s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 22nd (1min 6s behind Mas)
  • Stage 9: 11th (1min 44s behind Mas)

Harold Tejada

Harold Tejada is enjoying his best Grand Tour to date, it seems. He’s been hanging on up the climbs, and the Colombian finds himself inside the top ten for the first time in his Grand Tour career.

Tejada has been in strong form this year, with top tens at Paris-Nice and the UAE Tour. He’s by no means a traditional GC rider, but he’s been there or thereabouts on many stages of Grand Tours over the past few years.

XDS Astana are one of the stronger teams at the minute, with Cristian Rodríguez looking particularly strong. It would take a lot for Tejada to end up on the podium, but it’s not completely out of the realm of possibility. XDS Astana have been playing a blinder for the past two seasons, don’t forget.

Harald Tejada overview

  • Current position overall: 8th (4min 39sec)
  • Best result in a Grand Tour: 12th (Vuelta a España 2025)
  • Best result in the Vuelta a España: 12th (2025)

Harald Tejada’s key stage results so far

  • Stage 1: 59th (3s behind Mas)
  • Stage 4: 13th (1min 55s behind Mas)
  • Stage 6: 5th (46s behind Mas)
  • Stage 7: 27th (1min behind Mas)
  • Stage 9: 8th (33s behind Mas)
